raw_response.overlap_rationale: Both papers are readable qualitative fieldwork studies of domestic piped water services in Abuja, Nigeria, conducted by Ismaila Rimi Abubakar, and exhibit clear partial sample overlap. Study B (2016) analyzes interviews conducted between 2013 and 2015 with 85 adult piped-water residents across 14 residential districts (25 Phase I, 32 Phase II, 28 Phase III; 53 male, 32 female) plus 30 city water/engineering officials. Study A (2018) analyzes interviews conducted in summer 2015 with 60 household heads or spouses across 12 residential districts (~23 Phase I, ~20 Phase II, ~17 Phase III; 44 male, 16 female) and no officials. Critically, both papers describe the exact same initial seed of 18 key informants with at least 10 years of residency in Abuja, the exact same three snowball-sampling eligibility criteria (adult/household head or spouse, piped water connection at home, and >=3 years at current residence), the exact same respondent residency span (3 to 28 years), and an overlapping 2015 fieldwork window, with every geographic and gender subgroup count in Study A fitting as a subset within Study B's 85-resident sample while excluding Study B's 25 additional residents and 30 city officials. Although Study A cites Study B as an earlier study and focuses on household coping strategies and regulatory/socioeconomic determinants rather than Study B's seven utility service-quality and governance dimensions, both draw on overlapping Abuja household interview data and report overlapping observations on spatial inequity across city phases, flat-rate billing, water quality/treatment, and vending/fetching.
raw_response.study_a_sample_and_data: Qualitative semi-structured face-to-face interviews and direct observations conducted in summer 2015 with N = 60 piped-water households (44 male household heads, 16 female spouses; residency 3-28 years, mean 9 years) across 12 residential districts in Phases I (38%), II (33%) and III (28%) of Abuja City, Nigeria, recruited from 18 key informants (>=10 years residency) via snowball sampling.
raw_response.study_b_sample_and_data: Qualitative semi-structured interviews and field observations conducted between 2013 and 2015 in Abuja City, Nigeria, with N = 115 interviewees comprising 85 piped-water residents (53 male, 32 female; residency 3-28 years, mean ~10 years) across 14 residential districts in Phases I (n = 25), II (n = 32) and III (n = 28)—recruited from 18 participating key informants (>=10 years residency) via snowball sampling—plus 30 city officials from the Abuja Water Board (18) and FCTA engineering department (12).
